title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: It was a warm, dark autumn night. It had been raining for four days. Having changed horses twice and galloped twenty miles in an hour and a half over a sticky, muddy road, Bolkhovitinov reached Litashevka after one in the morning. Dismounting at a cottage on whose wattle fence hung a sign reading GENERAL STAFF, he threw down his reins and entered a dark corridor.
'The general on duty—quickly! It's very important!' he said to someone who had risen and was sniffing in the dark passage.
'He's been very unwell since this evening, and this is the third night he hasn't slept,' the orderly whispered pleadingly. 'You should wake the captain first.'
'But this is very important—from General Dokhturov,' said Bolkhovitinov, finding the open door by feeling in the dark.
The orderly went in ahead and began waking someone.
'Your honor! Your honor! A courier!'
'What? What's that? From whom?' came a sleepy voice.
'From Dokhturov and Alexei Petrovich. Napoleon is at Forminsk,' said Bolkhovitinov, unable to see who was speaking in the dark but guessing from the voice that it wasn't Konovnitsyn.
The man who had been woken yawned and stretched.
'I don't like waking him,' he said, fumbling for something. 'He's very ill. Maybe this is just a rumor.'
'Here's the dispatch,' said Bolkhovitinov. 'My orders are to deliver it immediately to the general on duty.'

'Wait a moment, I'll light a candle. Where do you always hide the damn thing, you rascal?' said the voice of the stretching man to the orderly. (This was Shcherbinin, Konovnitsyn's adjutant.) 'I've found it, I've found it!' he added.
The orderly was striking a light, and Shcherbinin was fumbling for the candlestick.
'Oh, the disgusting creatures!' he said with revulsion.
By the light of the sparks, Bolkhovitinov saw Shcherbinin's youthful face as he held the candle, and the face of another man still asleep. This was Konovnitsyn.

When the flame of the sulfur splinter, kindled by the tinderbox, flared first blue then red, Shcherbinin lit the tallow candle—from which cockroaches that had been gnawing on it scurried away—and looked at the messenger. Bolkhovitinov was splattered all over with mud and had smeared his face by wiping it with his sleeve.
'Who sent the report?' asked Shcherbinin, taking the envelope.
'The intelligence is reliable,' said Bolkhovitinov. 'Prisoners, Cossacks, and scouts all confirm the same thing.'

'There's nothing for it—we'll have to wake him,' said Shcherbinin, rising and walking over to the man in the nightcap who lay covered by a greatcoat. 'Pyotr Petrovich!' he said. (Konovnitsyn didn't stir.) 'To the General Staff!' he said with a smile, knowing those words were sure to rouse him.

And indeed, the head in the nightcap lifted at once. On Konovnitsyn's handsome, resolute face, with cheeks flushed from fever, there lingered for a moment a faraway, dreamy expression—then he suddenly snapped to attention, and his face took on its usual calm, firm look.
'Well, what is it? From whom?' he asked immediately, without hurry, blinking at the light.

While listening to the officer's report, Konovnitsyn broke the seal and read the dispatch. He had barely finished before he lowered his legs in their woolen stockings to the dirt floor and began pulling on his boots. Then he took off his nightcap, combed his hair over his temples, and put on his cap.
'Did you get here quickly? Let's go to His Highness.'

Konovnitsyn had understood at once that this news was of great importance and that there was no time to lose. He didn't pause to consider whether it was good news or bad. That didn't interest him. He viewed the entire business of the war not through intelligence or reason but through something deeper. Within him lay a deep, unspoken conviction that all would be well—but that one must not rely on this, much less talk about it. One must simply attend to one's own work. And he did his work, giving it his full strength.

Pyotr Petrovich Konovnitsyn, like Dokhturov, seems to have been included merely for form's sake in the list of the so-called heroes of 1812—the Barclays, Raevskys, Ermolovs, Platovs, and Miloradoviches. Like Dokhturov, he had the reputation of being a man of very limited abilities, and like Dokhturov, he never drew up battle plans but was always found where things were most difficult. Since his appointment as general on duty, he always slept with his door open, with orders that every messenger be allowed to wake him. In battle he was always under fire, so that Kutuzov reproached him for it and was afraid to send him to the front. And like Dokhturov, he was one of those unnoticed cogs that, without noise or fuss, form the most essential parts of the machine.

Emerging from the hut into the damp, dark night, Konovnitsyn frowned—partly from a worsening pain in his head and partly at the unpleasant thought of how all those influential men on the staff would be stirred up by this news, especially Bennigsen, who had been at war with Kutuzov ever since Tarutino. He could already picture their suggestions, their quarrels, their orders and counter-orders. This prospect was disagreeable, though he knew it couldn't be avoided.

And indeed, Toll—the first person he went to with the news—immediately began laying out his plans to a general sharing his quarters, until Konovnitsyn, who had been listening in weary silence, reminded him that they needed to go see His Highness.
